subject: The loonie two-month low lands on your mortgage
bodyMarkdown:
If you have a mortgage coming up for renewal, Thursday was a bad day, and the reason has almost nothing to do with Canada. That is exactly why I do not think it fixes itself quickly.

## The loonie fell for a fourth straight day

FXStreet reported on Thursday that the Canadian dollar fell for a fourth session in a row, pushing USD/CAD above 1.4100 and to about 1.4141, its weakest in two months. The shove came from south of the border. Yahoo Finance reported on Thursday that the US 10-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.116 per cent, and money goes where it gets paid more. CNBC reported that the Fed raised its target range a quarter point to 3.75 to 4.00 per cent on September 16, its first increase since 2023, with Chair Kevin Warsh saying inflation has been "too high ... for too long." The Bank of Canada held at 2.25 per cent on September 2. At the midpoints that is a gap of 162.5 **basis points** (a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point), up from 137.5 before the Fed moved. Brent crude above $105 normally lifts the loonie. It did not this week.

## What that does to a renewal

Canadian fixed mortgage rates do not follow the Bank of Canada. They follow the five-year Government of Canada bond, and Trading Economics has that yield rising to 3.72 per cent on Thursday, up four basis points on the day and near a 52-week high. It sat at 2.72 per cent in late February. Ratehub currently lists the best five-year fixed at 4.09 per cent, and counts more than 1.15 million Canadian mortgages renewing this year, most of them signed in 2020 and 2021 at rates between 1.49 and 2.29 per cent. Ratehub estimates a borrower renewing off a five-year fixed could see payments rise about $622 a month, or 24 per cent. The American version is worse. TheStreet reported on Thursday, citing Mortgage News Daily, that the average 30-year US mortgage rate jumped 11 basis points in a single day to 7.37 per cent, the highest since May 2024.

## The Bank of Canada is boxed in

Cutting would be the obvious response if inflation were behaving. It is not. Statistics Canada put August inflation at 3.0 per cent, unchanged from July, with gasoline up 22.8 per cent from a year earlier as the Middle East conflict keeps oil supply tight. The economy is not asking for rescue either, with real GDP growing at a 3.3 per cent annualized pace in the second quarter. The 50 per cent tariffs the two countries now levy on each other push prices up, not down, and the Bank's September 2 statement named both the energy shock and the new tariffs as upside risks to inflation. So a cut would weaken the loonie further and import more inflation through everything Canadians buy in US dollars, while a hold keeps the yield gap wide and the currency soft. Neither door is a good one. The next decision is October 28.

## The takeaway

If you renew in the next six months, get a rate hold this week, because most lenders hold for 90 to 120 days and the five-year yield is sitting near a 52-week high rather than a low. Watch that five-year Government of Canada yield rather than the Bank of Canada headline, since it is the number that actually sets your fixed rate. The pattern breaks if oil comes down, and Thursday's market coverage said US and Iranian negotiators are working toward a phased deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to shipping. Until that lands, I would plan on the gap staying wide through October 28.
